tweets.text:
Amazon $AMZN shares down almost 6% after-hours as earnings miss and capex soars accelerating its cash flow burn.

That was despite AWS growing 39.3% to $46.0B, its fastest in nearly five years and above the $45.29B consensus (TipRanks), although short of the ~42% buyside whisper (ZeroHedge). Jassy now projects 40%+ AWS growth in both 2027 and 2028.  

But:
▪️ Net capex of $75.9B vs. $42.4B of operating cash flow = a $33.5B cash burn in one quarter. Bloomberg consensus was a $7.7B outflow (per ZeroHedge) 
▪️ Trailing 12-month free cash flow: −$42.4B, from −$7.6B in Q2 
▪️ $48.1B of new long-term debt in Q3; long-term debt now $173.1B vs. $65.6B at the end of 2025 
▪️ Interest expense more than tripled to $1.7B and now exceeds Amazon's $1.2B of interest income 
▪️ Holding the $220B 2026 capex plan implies ~$47.8B in Q4, 37% below Q3. Either spending slows sharply, or the $220B estimate gets blown through  

Weak spots under the beat: 
▪️ AWS added $3.75B of revenue from Q2, vs. $4.65B the quarter before (despite an extra day), and its margin slipped to 38.7% from 39.4% 
▪️AWS lagged its peers: Azure +48%, Google Cloud +103% (including TPU sales). Google Cloud added ~$15.5B of revenue year over year, more than AWS's $13.0B, from a base less than half the size.
▪️ Ads +12% ex-currency, $19.64B vs. $20.82B est. Amazon blames Prime Day timing, but Q2 and Q3 combined grew 18.1% vs. 23.2% over the same stretch last year 
▪️ The record 13.9% operating margin is mix: every segment's margin fell from Q2 
▪️ Operating income +61% year over year is actually +29% vs. last year's figure excluding the FTC and severance charges  

Q3 Revenue $201.9B vs. $202.31B est.; EPS $1.89 vs. $1.96 (TipRanks). 

Q4 guide: sales $240B to $247B (FactSet consensus $244.17B); operating income $28.5B to $33.5B, a $31B midpoint vs. ~$33B Street.

tweets.text:
Intel ($INTC) shares down around 16% after-hours despite a Q3 beat as current quarter guidance came in well below expectations.  

Q3 vs. TipRanks consensus:
▪️ Adj. EPS 52c vs. 41c expected
▪️ Revenue $16.51B (+21%) vs. $16.56B 
▪️ Non-GAAP gross margin 44.1%, vs. 42.0%

Q4 guidance vs consensus
▪️ Revenue $15B–$16B vs. $17.06B. Midpoint 9% below, −6% q/q 
▪️ Adj. EPS 25c vs. 44c 
▪️ Gross margin guided to 38.0%, down 6.1 pts from Q3   

Data represented all the growth: 
▪️ Data Center & AI +78% to $7.3B (fastest in 15 years), vs. $6.7B expected per MarketWatch 
▪️ It supplied 112% of Intel's $2.86B revenue gain. Ex-data center, sales FELL 3.6% 
▪️ Segment op margin 41.5% vs. 23.4% a year ago ▪️ PC chips −5% to $8.1B vs. $8.9B expected, −9% q/q  

Intel blames memory-driven PC weakness it says will last through at least 1H 2027 and an Israel fab disruption (explosion, per MarketWatch). 

It sees the PC market −10% in 2027 after −12% in 2026 (Bloomberg).  

Inventory rose 4.6% q/q to $13.1B into a PC downturn.  

So the AI CPU demand is real, and data center is now Intel's profit engine. But a stock up 140%+ this year (FT) was priced for a smoother transition, and a guide that cuts revenue, margin and EPS at once isn't one.

tweets.text:
Brian Schimpf of @AndurilTech on why industrial production is a deterrent in itself, and why technological superiority alone won't win a war:

"These wars are protracted, they are industrial in scale, and if you were to bring it down to one variable, the amount of kilograms that you can throw at each other turns out to probably be the single most important factor."

"I think the technical superiority is a huge advantage. We're not gonna just outproduce China on like dumb ammunition, right? Like that clearly we have to have an edge around our space capabilities, how we can sense, how we can confuse them, how sophisticated our weapons are."

"But I think the part that got so clear outta Ukraine was that industrial production has a deterrence factor... it is critical for winning a conflict."

"When most of the war games with China show that we'd be out of munitions in... like eight days, that's not a deterrence factor really anymore."

"I think the belief for a long time was that [technological superiority] was sufficient, but a low number of really exquisite weapons is not gonna win a conflict."

@SchimpfBrian (September 2025)

a16z's Erin Price-Wright says factory technicians can now retool production lines with AI in 20 minutes, a job that used to take an outside integrator 3 months:

"Historically, if you're setting up a line with a lot of automation, you really need to be producing a lot of one single thing. That's how you get the cost down, and how you justify investing in a pretty bespoke manufacturing line."

"But what we're seeing across our portfolio is that manufacturing technicians themselves have the intuition, and now the software tools, to change the economics of producing low-volume, high-mix on the line."

"A manufacturing technician, not necessarily someone with a college degree or who's studied software engineering, can now use these tools to reprogram and reconfigure their lines on the fly, because they understand the manufacturing process."

"Instead of calling a systems integrator, which takes 3 months and hundreds of thousands of dollars to reconfigure a line, you can have a manufacturing engineer use Claude and do that in 20 minutes. That's been a real game changer."

@espricewright

a16z's Connor Love says building for defense is how America builds for everything else, because once you can make the parts "to quality and to cost," new markets start to make sense:

"When you build many systems, you also require many subsystems below that. There are really interesting military systems being built today. The corollary: by building towards defense, you also build for a different industry."

"The subsystems that go into some of our military systems are the exact same subsystems that are going to go into the future robotic systems. It's the actuators, the motors, the valves and switches."

"When you can build those to quality and to cost, then all of a sudden other markets that maybe weren't viable make sense... You're going to have this robotic wave that will come in America."

"AI can't turn a wrench yet. They will eventually. And that will be enabled by all that, actuators and switches and subsystems that we built... And we're not going to have to rely on factories in China."

"As you build an industrial base, an industrial base can be used for many things. Down to the component level, I just think we don’t have enough of it in America."

@ConnorLoveCA @espricewright @VirtualElena

And if you look at how Elon and his team have built those businesses, it's been, one, very vertically integrated."

"I take the ideology that you shouldn't vertically integrate everything. I mean, again, if you're building a super exquisite system like a missile that is doing something very unique, you kind of have to because you have to control the exquisiteness. You have to control the cost."

Erin: "SpaceX and Tesla were doing first of their kind. There didn't exist an industrial base in the US to support them, and so they had to build it themselves. I think where there are high-quality suppliers, you should use suppliers."

Connor: "In a lot of ways they had to make those choices because they didn't have any other opportunity. But in the end, it's actually just that mantra of design for manufacturing that now exists within all these systems companies."

@ConnorLoveCA @espricewright

Demand for Bitcoin is rising again.

It’s time to teach people how to believe in something again.

tweets.text:
Power has become a harder constraint on AI than chips.

A 1 GW data center waiting on power loses about $8 million a day to chip depreciation alone. That cost is pushing developers to pay up for fuel cells, build gas plants on site and run generators made from retired jet engines.

Most of those are stopgaps until a large gas turbine comes free. GE Vernova’s backlog has reached about six years of output. The wait is long enough that SpaceX plans to cast its own turbine blades.

On-site gas and fuel cells fill the gap for the next few years. The largest tech companies are also paying up for clean power to take over after that. Google agreed in October to pay more than double the cost of a new gas plant for extra output from existing nuclear reactors.

Some are betting even further out on advanced reactors, next-generation geothermal and fusion power that has never reached the grid.

The demand behind those bets is still climbing. Data centers used under 5% of U.S. electricity in 2024. Forecasts for 2030 now run as high as 17% and keep getting revised up.

Anyone who can deliver power faster than the grid will be able to charge for it.

#Uranium #Copper #Silver #Gold
⚡ THE DAILY METALS PULSE | 29 OCTOBER 2026
Inflation heats up. Precious metals slide. Kazakhstan moves toward a strategic uranium reserve.
A day when the macro headlines and the physical markets both deserve attention. 👇

🌍 MACRO: Today’s releases showed US Q3 growth accelerating to 3.4% annualised, while September PCE inflation rose 0.5% month-on-month and 3.6% year-on-year. Core inflation remained at 3.1%.

Growth gives the Fed room to stay tough. Inflation gives it a reason.

The ECB also held today, keeping its deposit rate at 2.5% while warning that higher energy costs threaten both inflation and growth.

🟡 GOLD: Spot around $4,009/oz, down 1.4%. The inflation hedge is feeling the pressure of the policy response: markets still priced roughly an 80% chance of a December Fed hike.

⚪ SILVER: Around $52.08/oz, down 3.5%. A sharper retreat than gold as precious metals headed toward a second consecutive monthly decline.

🔶 COPPER: AI spending concerns weighed on sentiment, while US COMEX inventories were up 60% this year. Meanwhile, China’s Yangshan import premium reached $205/t yesterday, its highest in over a decade. The location of available metal matters enormously.

☢️ URANIUM: Kazakhstan’s prime minister today instructed state bodies to establish a strategic uranium reserve for future domestic reactors.

The announcement does not establish how much uranium will be reserved or when. But the policy direction is significant: long-term fuel security is becoming a national priority even in a major uranium-producing country.

Who controls tomorrow’s available supply is becoming an increasingly important question.

We got flying cars, now it's time we get a modern financial system.

Let me Coinbase-pill you for a minute. Financial services is a massive industry. All fintech companies combined capture about 4% of total global financial-services revenues, while traditional financial-services companies account for the remaining ~96%.

Crypto is replacing the rails: stablecoins let anyone move money anywhere, instantly and almost free; tokenization lets anyone own any asset; and onchain markets let them trade it around the clock.

Together they can give every person and business the financial power that used to belong to a few. Coinbase exists to make that happen in a way people can trust.

Coinbase is using these frontier technologies to build the best modern financial account. Crypto rails, AI interface. Trading, payments, saving, borrowing, etc all in one.

Some Q3 highlights:
- We store more crypto than anyone in the world
- We have a global regulatory foundation with 80+ licenses
- 14th consecutive ATH of average USDC in CB products
- 5th consecutive ATH in CB1 subs

Best of all, the everything exchange is working. The progress since we announced last year has been awesome:
- 4th quarter of crypto trading volume market share gains, nearly doubled since this time last year
- $200M+ annualized revenue from prediction markets in Q3, one of our fastest growing products by revenue in history! With >60% daily trader growth QoQ

Jobs not finished until the entire financial system is updated with these frontier technologies.

$SYHBF $SYH.V #Uranium #Nuclear
One date in Skyharbour’s latest update caught my attention: 1989. ⚒️

That’s when the Little Man area at Getty East was last drilled before the current campaign.

Historical drilling outlined uranium mineralization along 500 metres. Skyharbour’s interpretation suggests it remains open in both directions, with the underlying basement rocks entirely untested.

Now Denison is funding a ~3,600m Getty East drill program, operated by Skyharbour, with four holes initially planned at Little Man.

Think about that: a known uranium occurrence, geological questions left unanswered for decades, and fresh drilling to investigate them.

The deeper exploration theme extends to the 100%-owned Moore project, where the 2026 program includes testing largely unexplored basement potential around Maverick’s high-grade mineralization.

That’s an aspect of $SYH I find particularly interesting. Modern exploration models can bring a different perspective to ground where earlier drilling established that uranium was present—and left plenty unresolved.

The drill bit still has to deliver. But these are concrete geological questions worth testing as the nuclear industry looks toward its future fuel needs.

Looking forward to @JordanPTrimble’s full RCTV interview. There’s a lot to discuss beneath the surface of Skyharbour’s Athabasca story.

Paid partnership with Skyharbour Resources.

The core promise of crypto has always been efficient value transfer, and for the first time we are seeing broad uptake of these systems. 

The last few years we were in the experimental phase, similar to the internet boom of the early 2000s. There was building across the board of similar products and it paid to own the smaller assets as everything was promise -- nothing truly worked. 

Now that we have successfully built systems that *work*, they are getting integrated at lightning pace and the next few years we will see a radical transformation of the entire financial system. 

This means value will accrue to the set of assets that are currently winning. Partnerships now mean something. Users are stickier. Underwriting and research actually matter. 

Instead of looking downstream, build conviction and concrete in the best assets. They will continue to compound and win.

People ask why I don’t run a subscription service. The truth is, people who make real money don’t need one.

My personal account has grown from five figures to seven figures, and it keeps getting closer to eight figures. Hopefully, it gets there very soon. I built it through 15 years of hard work, deep thought, and constant learning. I’m always evolving and improving.

I’d rather share what I know for free than try to make even more money from subscriptions. When people with serious money want to work with me, they reach out. I sometimes take on new clients, but generally, what I do for myself, I share here too.

I don’t publish every trade, of course. I often use ratio spreads in this market, for example, and I’ve explained the concept and how I choose the strikes. I also know my stocks well, so when they draw down, I’m not too worried as long as the story hasn’t changed.

Z is, and always will be, knowledge for free.

A big choice in life is accomplishment versus savoring life.

Savoring life is taking a moment to smell the roses, enjoying a beautiful day, and making sure you have time with the people you love. Then there's the other side, which is accomplishment and impact.

You have to discover for yourself where you are and how you deal with those choices. The key, and the most effective path, is where they align—when you can make your work and your passion one and the same.

Here's the thing about fundraising that nobody talks about:

Many VCs won't even look at your deck unless someone they trust sends it to them.

At @DraperVC any founder can pitch us directly through our site.

We've already made 3 investments this year from founders who just... showed up in our inbox.

But here's what I keep seeing...

Founders spend weeks perfecting their pitch deck, only to receive their first real feedback when they're sitting across from an investor.

That's like practicing your wedding speech in front of the wedding guests.

So we built something called PitchLens.

It's an AI pitch coach trained on how we actually evaluate deals at Draper.

It'll tell you:
→ Where your story gets confusing
→ Which slides aren't pulling their weight
→ How to tighten your narrative before you hit send

tweets.text:
re: the “communist/socialist” boogeyman in America

what’s interesting is you see a lot of Republican candidates pushing this messaging as a way to discredit Democratic challengers in races across the country (especially at the national level)

but it’s not really detracting from their appeal anymore. why?

the terms communism, socialism, etc. had much greater relevance to people in prior decades due to the Soviet threat. everyone associated communism with the USSR. and there was very little integration and trade between the US and USSR

but ofc, the USSR no longer exists. so what about China? aren’t they communist?

sort of, but to people sitting in the US, China actually comes across as hyper-capitalist (albeit authoritarian), especially on the global stage. i.e., people buy a ton of Chinese products (knowingly and unknowingly) and know that they are now maybe the greatest physically productive nation on the planet today

so the terms “communist” and “socialist” don’t have the same negative connotation they once had. we’re a full generation past the collapse of the USSR. and the one great power which is called “communist” seems to not be collapsing under its own weight

combine this with the specter of AI-related job losses and you can see why these ideologies are becoming more appealing to more people, especially when people can see that the government is increasingly corrupt and their cost of living is getting much worse relative to their wages

i don’t think socialism as it’s conceived of by organizations such as the DSA is the answer at all, but you’d have to be blind not to see that we need revisions to our economic model if it cannot sustain a thriving middle class of workers (especially in the face of greater destruction of that middle class through AI). even Elon seems to acknowledge this by talking about “universal high income”

the longer it takes us to start having these discussions, the more calamitous it will be once the boiling point is reached

anyway, don’t shoot the messenger…

Quick more detailed rundown

- Midterms: blue wave, little vol priced in, unimportant, who takes the senate makes little diff for markets (key for nominations), though headlines will be big
- Iran: huge short-term, Trump threatening action post midterms, Likud did better than expected, may have gridlock for a while, so Netanyahu's urgency fades
- Earnings: major risk short term, no edge, many stocks attractive to me here on a 3 months window (like meta at these levels in particular)
- Rates: long the long end as hedge for growth scares
- Fiscal: steady issuance, expect Bessent to shift supply from the long end to the short end of the belly
- Monetary: 1 hike in Dec, though this is baked in, the entire front end has a lot priced-in into 2027, and the FOMC voting composition shifts dovish in Jan

TLDR all about earnings, 2027 capex, and Iran/energy prices

Think the trade is to fade capex/earnings fears and a hawkish Fed from early Dec or once Iran clears. Before then we are in the earnings/Iran lottery period and ideal for fast traders. Long the long end is a great trade up to Q1 inclusive (a debt ceiling episode will hit in H2)

ok safe to say binance is pwned

The biggest assets were approximately:

• 1.615B USDT
• 62.6M RLUSD
• 29,934 wBETH
• 11,372 XAUt
• 6.19M UNI
• 198.4M ENA
• 7.175T PEPE
• 27.8M USD1
• 2.26M LINK
• 127,853 AAVE

about $2.5B at the explorer’s prices.

1. The attacker deployed a delegate contract, 0x63e842b0...73e9c6fAe, from the relayer at 15:59 UTC.

2. About four hours later, the relayer submitted an EIP-7702 authorization transaction

That installed the malicious 7702 delegate code on Binance 14. 

3. The relayer then made a call to Binance 14, executing the delegate code, and transferring Binance 14’s ETH and token balances.

4. The calldata is labeled sweep(address, address[]). The second argument is a list of recognizable token-contract addresses plus the zero-address (eth).

5. The same relayer later used the same delegate to move 780M USDC from Binance Hot Wallet 34 into the same pool

• The relayer 0x7C... was funded by three Tornado Cash 0.1 ETH withdrawals over the prior two days.
• The same pool also received 28,005.6 ETH from Binance 16 24 seconds after the main sweep.
• The pool then forwarded 195,460 ETH to a fresh, unlabeled EOA
• That EOA has only one transaction and currently holds the 195,460 ETH.

What's a bit unclear is why the relayer was needed in the first place. If they had the private keys to the Binance wallets, they could have just sent the assets out in an atomic bundle without needing a relayer at all. 

So it seems likely that they didn't have the private keys and instead just had the 7702 auth signatures, which must have been phished somehow. 

I think we can go ahead and assume DPRK.

Growing up in the United States, NYSE was synonymous with the story of American capitalism. I vividly remember learning about the Buttonwood agreement in 9th grade history class. 24 stockbrokers met under a tree on Wall Street and formed the beginning of what would become the world's financial center. From pits to computers to now onchain markets, America has always led the way in innovating markets to improve price discovery and capital formation. Today the next chapter begins with ICE, trade[XYZ], and Hyperliquid.

ICE started as an electricity-trading platform in 2000, growing to acquire NYSE itself in only 13 years. It is a key infrastructure provider of America’s energy, bond, and mortgage markets. ICE is a rare story of exponential growth of a financial giant over decades, continually embracing innovation and technology.

trade[XYZ] was the first HIP-3 deployer and responsible for spearheading the flourishing global RWA perpetual market today. Only a year ago, trade[XYZ] launched its first RWA perpetual markets. They took a bet on HIP-3, which had just launched after months of tireless development. Having followed their journey from day 1, I cannot overstate how much Shoku and the team have poured into growing these markets to a genuine source of price discovery for the most important assets in the world.

Over the past three years, Hyperliquid has pioneered onchain infrastructure to house all of finance. Hyperliquid is nothing without its world-class builders. I am honored that trade[XYZ] and ICE have chosen to build on Hyperliquid to bring perpetual contracts to America.

When I first spoke to Jeff Sprecher around a year ago, he asked what success looks like to me. I thought for some time and joked that it would be seeing ICE building on Hyperliquid's technology. I could never have predicted the progress that we've made as a community in a single year to make this come true. Excited to see what we can build together next.

Ok, I'll bite. I grew up in Montreal and I want Canada to win in AI. I'm just not sure if this is actually good for Canadian AI industry/startup ecosystem.

- idk how canada as the lead investor is a good thing/signal for the canadian ecosystem.

- It tells young founders the way to win here is to get close to Ottawa.

- When the government owns part of a company, every other Canadian AI startup is now competing with a company their own government owns. 

 - "We're not American" works as a pitch in almost every country except the biggest market in the world. Would love to see more Canadian startups be #1 globally like how Shopify is a great model.

- How Canadian is the "Canadian champion" after a German retailer leads the round and it merges with a German company?

- Does "sovereign" mean the models are built in Canada, or just hosted there?

- Why share 165% ARR growth but not what the ARR actually is?

- What does the government’s stake come with, like a board seat or a say in decisions?

Congrats on the round, its massive but just thinking about the Canadian ecosystem and what's best for it
